title: History of Life: Transitions, Extinctions and Radiations

generated.pipeline: extract → Opus draft → Sonnet accuracy gate → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: {{c1::Macroevolution}} is evolution above the species level: the origin, diversification and extinction of species and larger groups.
cards.quote: Macroevolution is evolution above the species level: the origin, diversification and extinction of species and larger groups, built from the processes in speciation and molecular evolution.

cards.front: In a simple birth-death model of lineages, with speciation rate λ and extinction rate μ, the net diversification rate is {{c1::r = λ − μ}}.
cards.back: Births minus deaths of lineages.
cards.quote: The net rate is r = λ − μ: births minus deaths of lineages.

cards.front: Why can a slowly changing count of lineages not tell you the speciation and extinction rates behind it?
cards.back: The same slow net change can come from two high rates that nearly cancel or from two low ones; the count reflects only their difference.
cards.quote: A slowly changing count can hide two high rates that nearly cancel, or two low ones; the count alone cannot tell which.

cards.front: Illustrative rates: λ = 0.20 and μ = 0.19 per lineage per million years. About how long does an average lineage last, and how long does the expected count take to double?
cards.back: Lifetime about 1/μ = 1/0.19, about 5 million years. Net rate r = 0.01, so doubling takes ln 2 / 0.01, about 69 million years.
cards.why: Turnover is fast; net change is slow.
cards.quote: At that pace the expected count doubles in about 69 million years (ln 2 / 0.01; ln 2 is about 0.69).

cards.front: With illustrative rates λ = 0.20 and μ = 0.19 per lineage per million years, how long does the expected count take to recover after losing three-quarters of its species?
cards.back: One-quarter is left, so recovery means growing fourfold: ln 4 / 0.01, about 139 million years on the average path.
cards.why: Any one real clade is subject to chance and can follow a very different path or die out.
cards.quote: Refilling a loss of three-quarters of species means growing fourfold, about 139 million years (ln 4 / 0.01) on that average path

cards.front: After a mass extinction removes three-quarters of a clade's species, the survivors speciate at λ = 0.25 per lineage per million years while μ stays at 0.19 (illustrative). About how long does the expected count take to refill, compared with about 139 million years at λ = 0.20?
cards.back: r = 0.25 − 0.19 = 0.06. Fourfold growth takes ln 4 / 0.06, about 23 million years: roughly six times faster.
cards.why: Rests on r = λ − μ: recovering faster needs a larger net rate. This is the expected path; real clades vary by chance.
cards.quote: Recovering faster needs a larger net rate: more speciation, less extinction, or both.

cards.front: What is a mass extinction?
cards.back: A short interval when species are lost far faster than new ones arise.
cards.quote: A mass extinction is a short interval when species are lost far faster than new ones arise.

cards.front: What is an adaptive radiation?
cards.back: The rapid diversification of one lineage into types adapted to different ecological niches (a niche is the set of conditions and resources a type uses).
cards.quote: An adaptive radiation is the rapid diversification of one lineage into types adapted to different ecological niches

cards.front: A clade's species count falls over 10 million years. A student concludes that extinction rose. What other change in rates could produce the same drop?
cards.back: Speciation stalling: a fall in λ with μ unchanged also lowers r = λ − μ. The count alone cannot tell the two apart.
cards.quote: And a drop in diversity can come from speciation stalling as well as from extinction rising.

cards.front: What does the Great Oxidation Event (GOE) refer to, and what does it not refer to?
cards.back: The first significant buildup of oxygen in the atmosphere: when oxygen accumulated, not when oxygenic photosynthesis began.
cards.quote: The Great Oxidation Event (GOE) is the first significant buildup of oxygen in the atmosphere: when oxygen accumulated, not when oxygenic photosynthesis began
cards.section: Major transitions: new lineages, and a new atmosphere

cards.front: Name three things the Great Oxidation Event changed for life.
cards.back: Aerobic metabolisms expanded; an ozone layer formed that would have shielded organisms in shallow surface environments from ultraviolet light; organisms had to contend with the harmful effects of free oxygen.
cards.quote: Aerobic metabolisms expanded, an ozone layer formed that would have shielded organisms in shallow surface environments from ultraviolet light
cards.section: Major transitions: new lineages, and a new atmosphere

cards.front: Order these, oldest first, with approximate dates: animals, plants on land, microbial life, a many-celled alga, eukaryotes, onset of the Great Oxidation Event.
cards.back: Microbial life by about 3.48 Ga; GOE onset about 2,460 to 2,426 Ma; eukaryotes by 1.9 to 1.4 Ga; a many-celled alga (Bangiomorpha) by about 1.05 Ga; animals by about 558 Ma; plants on land by about 473 to 471 Ma.
cards.quote: Eukaryotes (cells with a nucleus) by 1.9 to 1.4 Ga; a many-celled alga by about 1.05 Ga.
cards.section: Major transitions: new lineages, and a new atmosphere

cards.front: Animal sterols are dominated by cholesterol and its relatives. Bobrovskiy and colleagues extracted the chemical remains of such molecules from organically preserved Dickinsonia. What did this show, and what did it not?
cards.back: It supported an animal affinity for Dickinsonia and its close relatives, but not for every fossil of the Ediacara biota (about 571 to 541 Ma).
cards.quote: The result supported an animal affinity for Dickinsonia and its close relatives, though not for every fossil of the Ediacara biota
cards.section: Major transitions: new lineages, and a new atmosphere

cards.front: Why is the date of a group's oldest fossil a minimum age rather than the date the group arose?
cards.back: Older traces could have been destroyed, never formed or not yet found. Preservation is uneven in space and time, so a gap in the record is not a gap in life.
cards.quote: The fossil entries are minimum ages: older traces could have been destroyed, never formed or not yet found.
cards.section: Major transitions: new lineages, and a new atmosphere

cards.front: How does the date for the onset of the Great Oxidation Event differ in kind from a fossil's date?
cards.back: It brackets an environmental change from both sides, using dated volcanic rocks. A fossil date is only a minimum age for a lineage.
cards.quote: The GOE entry instead brackets an environmental change from both sides, using dated volcanic rocks
cards.section: Major transitions: new lineages, and a new atmosphere

cards.front: A clade's oldest known fossil comes from rocks dated to 420 Ma. A new find pushes its oldest fossil back to 445 Ma. Does the new find contradict the earlier date?
cards.back: No. 420 Ma was a minimum age: the clade existed by then. The new find moves the minimum back to 445 Ma, and the clade may be older still.
cards.quote: Holland (2016) stressed that preservation is uneven in space and time, so a gap in the record is not a gap in life.
cards.section: Major transitions: new lineages, and a new atmosphere

cards.front: By the widely used benchmark, what loss makes a mass extinction, and how many have there been in about the past 540 million years?
cards.back: Loss of more than three-quarters of species in a geologically short interval. Five times, the Big Five: end-Ordovician, Devonian, Late Permian, Late Triassic and end-Cretaceous.
cards.quote: sets the bar at the loss of more than three-quarters of species in a geologically short interval
cards.section: Mass extinctions: when losses far outrun new species

cards.front: About the Big Five mass extinctions, what is debated and what is not?
cards.back: Not whether these intervals saw heavy losses. The debate is how sharply each stands out from background extinction and which intervals should count.
cards.quote: The debate is not over whether these intervals saw heavy losses but over how sharply each stands out from background extinction
cards.section: Mass extinctions: when losses far outrun new species

cards.front: What evidence led Schulte and colleagues (2010) to conclude that the Chicxulub impact, rather than the Deccan eruptions, triggered the end-Cretaceous mass extinction?
cards.back: A single ejecta-rich layer linked to Chicxulub is spread worldwide at the boundary, it matches the onset of the extinctions in time, and fossil patterns fit modelled darkness and cooling.
cards.quote: They weighed both causes and concluded that the Chicxulub impact triggered the mass extinction.
cards.section: Mass extinctions: when losses far outrun new species

cards.front: Iridium is scarce in Earth's crust but more abundant in many meteorites. End-Cretaceous boundary clay is iridium-enriched in Italy, Denmark and New Zealand. Why does finding it at widely separated sites matter more than finding it at one?
cards.back: One site could reflect a local accident of sedimentation; the same signal at widely separated sites makes that less likely. It does not by itself identify the cause.
cards.quote: The first film traced the evidence from iridium to the Chicxulub crater, with the Deccan eruptions in India as the rival cause.
cards.section: Mass extinctions: when losses far outrun new species

cards.front: Argon-argon dates place the Chicxulub impact and the end-Cretaceous extinction within 32,000 years of each other. What does this figure establish, and what would you need to learn how long the dying took?
cards.back: That impact and extinction happened at about the same time. It says nothing about how long the dying took; that needs dates within one rock section, as at Meishan.
cards.quote: Argon-argon dating by Renne and colleagues (2013) placed the impact and the extinction within 32,000 years of each other.
cards.section: Mass extinctions: when losses far outrun new species

cards.front: At Meishan, China, the end-Permian losses spanned about 60 ± 48 thousand years. A proposed kill mechanism would need about 1 million years of steady action to cause the losses. Does the Meishan dating weigh against it, and what can it not settle?
cards.back: It weighs against it at Meishan: the section's clock is tens of thousands of years, and any proposed cause must fit it. It cannot settle the kill mechanism or worldwide synchrony; it is one section.
cards.quote: That is one section: it constrains timing there, not the kill mechanism or worldwide synchrony, and gives a clock any proposed cause must fit.
cards.section: Mass extinctions: when losses far outrun new species

cards.front: In a rock section, the last fossils of many species disappear one by one over several metres below a layer marking an abrupt event. Does this show that the extinction was gradual?
cards.back: No. Most individuals leave no fossil, so a species' last fossil usually lies below where it vanished. A sudden extinction is smeared backwards and looks gradual: the Signor-Lipps effect.
cards.quote: a species' last fossil usually lies below where it actually vanished, so a sudden extinction is smeared backwards and looks gradual.
cards.section: Mass extinctions: when losses far outrun new species

cards.front: A leading candidate cause of adaptive radiation is {{c1::ecological opportunity}}: niches that no one is using.
cards.back: An extinction that removes the incumbents is one way to create it.
cards.quote: A leading candidate cause of adaptive radiation is ecological opportunity: niches that no one is using.
cards.section: Radiations: ecological opportunity in a flask and in the record

cards.front: Pseudomonas fluorescens populations started from one genotype diversify into several heritable types in unshaken microcosms but not in shaken ones. What supplied the ecological opportunity, and what kept the types present?
cards.back: Spatial structure, which shaking removes, supplied the opportunity. Competition among the niche specialists kept them all present.
cards.why: These are heritable morphs of an asexual bacterium, not new species. The flask tests the logic; it does not say every fossil radiation had the same cause.
cards.quote: In Rainey and Travisano's (1998) unshaken microcosms, spatial structure supplied the ecological opportunity, and competition among the niche specialists kept them all present.
cards.section: Radiations: ecological opportunity in a flask and in the record

cards.front: Placental mammal orders rose mainly after the end-Cretaceous extinction. Why is that timing consistent with release from competitors but not a test of it?
cards.back: Mammals were already diverse before the extinction, most molecular clocks place many splits among placental orders in the Cretaceous, and a coincident climate change could also explain the pattern.
cards.quote: is consistent with release from competitors (survivors freed from groups that had used the same resources) but does not test it
cards.section: Radiations: ecological opportunity in a flask and in the record

cards.front: What four things should you ask of any date in the history of life?
cards.back: The measured age, the method, its uncertainty, and whether it is a point, a bracket or a minimum age.
cards.quote: ask four things: the measured age, the method, its uncertainty, and whether it is a point, a bracket or a minimum age.
cards.section: How the dates are measured

cards.front: In radiometric dating with no initial daughter, the fraction of parent left is P / (P + D) = {{c1::(1/2)^n}}, where n is the number of half-lives elapsed.
cards.back: Age = n x half-life.
cards.quote: fraction of parent left = P / (P + D) = (1/2)^n, age = n x half-life
cards.section: How the dates are measured

cards.front: A closed zircon that started with no radiogenic lead has a daughter-to-parent ratio D/P = 3. Treating uranium-235 to lead-207 as one parent and one daughter with a half-life of 704 million years, what is its age?
cards.back: P0 = P + D = 4P, so 1/4 of the parent is left = (1/2)^2: n = 2. Age = 2 x 704 = 1,408 million years.
cards.why: Two half-lives, not three: D/P is not the number of half-lives.
cards.quote: Age = 2 x 704 million years = 1,408 million years, or 1.408 billion years.
cards.section: How the dates are measured

cards.front: A closed zircon with no initial radiogenic lead has D/P = 15. Using one parent and one daughter with a half-life of 704 million years, what is its age?
cards.back: P0 = P + 15P = 16P, so 1/16 is left = (1/2)^4: n = 4. Age = 4 x 704 = 2,816 million years.
cards.quote: Every daughter atom was once a parent atom, so P0 = P + D = P + 3P = 4P.
cards.section: How the dates are measured

cards.front: What assumptions does a simple radiometric age from D/P and a half-life rest on, and why does zircon meet the starting one?
cards.back: The mineral stayed closed (no parent or daughter entered or left), it started with no radiogenic daughter, and the half-life is fixed. Zircon takes up almost no lead when it forms.
cards.quote: because zircon takes up almost no lead when it forms, it started with no radiogenic lead.
cards.section: How the dates are measured

cards.front: A zircon lost some of its radiogenic lead after it formed, but its age is computed as if it had stayed closed. Is the computed age too old or too young, and why?
cards.back: Too young. The lost daughter lowers D/P, so the parent left looks like a larger fraction of the start, which means fewer half-lives.
cards.why: Rests on fraction left = P / (P + D) and the closed-system assumption.
cards.quote: A hypothetical zircon from an ash bed has stayed closed since it crystallized: no parent or daughter has entered or left
cards.section: How the dates are measured

cards.front: A fossil bed lies between two ash layers in undisturbed, right-way-up rock. The ash below is dated to 512 Ma and the ash above to 498 Ma. What can you say about the fossils' age?
cards.back: Younger than 512 Ma and older than 498 Ma. The lower layer is older, so the two dated ashes bracket the bed.
cards.quote: In undisturbed, right-way-up layers the lower one is older, so the fossils are younger than 1,450 and older than 1,408 million years.
cards.section: How the dates are measured

cards.front: How does a molecular clock date a divergence, and why must each fossil calibration be justified?
cards.back: It converts sequence differences among living species into divergence times, with fossils calibrating particular nodes. A misplaced or misdated fossil carries its error into the dates.
cards.quote: Molecular clocks convert sequence differences among living species into divergence times, with fossils calibrating particular nodes
cards.section: How the dates are measured

cards.front: A fossil calibrating a molecular clock was assigned an age 20% older than its rock really is. Assuming a constant clock, would the clock's other divergence dates come out too old or too young?
cards.back: Too old. A calibration's error carries into the other dates; under an assumed constant clock, an inflated calibration age implies a slower rate and stretches every date older.
cards.why: Rests on the rule that a misdated calibration fossil carries its error into the dates (Parham and colleagues, 2012).
cards.quote: because a misplaced or misdated fossil carries its error into the dates.
cards.section: How the dates are measured

cards.front: In a clade where λ and μ never changed and extinction was high, do new lineages appear on a time tree of its living species at a steady pace or faster toward the present, and why?
cards.back: Faster toward the present. Old lineages have had a long time to die out without living descendants, so most old branches are missing; young ones are nearly all still there. This is the pull of the present.
cards.quote: The count climbs steeply near today though the rates never changed: the pull of the present.
cards.section: What rates the record can and cannot give

cards.front: For a clade with constant λ = 0.20 and μ = 0.19 and every living species sampled, lineages split on the tree of living species at about 0.015 per lineage per million years 100 million years ago but 0.20 today. Why the difference, and what would μ = 0 give?
cards.back: Lineages that died out leave no tips, so old splits are under-counted; today every lineage is present, so the full λ shows. With no extinction there is no pull: splits appear at λ all the way back.
cards.quote: With no extinction there is no pull: lineages appear at the speciation rate all the way back.
cards.section: What rates the record can and cannot give

cards.front: Why can a tree of living species alone not tell steady rates with high extinction from speciation that rose recently with no extinction?
cards.back: Suitably matched versions of the two fit the tree exactly equally well. The missing information is the extinct side branches, so an assumption from outside the tree is needed.
cards.why: Under a general birth-death model, adding living species does not help (Louca and Pennell, 2020).
cards.quote: suitably matched versions of the two fit a tree of living species exactly equally well.
cards.section: What rates the record can and cannot give

cards.front: What does PyRate estimate, from what data, and why must it model preservation?
cards.back: Speciation and extinction rates, from dated fossil occurrences. Fossils are an incomplete record of extinct lineages, so it models how likely each lineage was to be preserved and found.
cards.quote: Silvestro and colleagues (2014) built a method, PyRate, that estimates speciation and extinction from dated fossil occurrences while modelling how likely each lineage was to be preserved and found.
cards.section: What rates the record can and cannot give

cards.front: Why can the Pseudomonas flask test ecological opportunity in a way the placental mammal radiation after the end-Cretaceous extinction cannot?
cards.back: The flask can be rerun with a control (shaken versus unshaken) that removes the opportunity while holding all else equal. The mammal event happened once, with a coincident climate change as a confound.
cards.why: Rests on the lesson's contrast between a repeatable experiment and a single event that can only be tested by dating and niche data.
cards.quote: Unlike the flask, this event cannot be rerun with a control.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A student claims the end-Cretaceous extinction caused the placental mammal radiation by removing competitors. What results from dated fossils and ecology would support the claim, and what would favour climate instead?
cards.back: Support: a rise in speciation starting at the extinction horizon, not before, and new mammal types taking the ecological roles of groups that died out. Climate: diversification timed to an independently dated climate shift.
cards.quote: Release from competitors predicts a rise in speciation that starts at the extinction horizon, not before it.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Molecular clocks calibrated with Bangiomorpha put the origin of the primary plastid at about 1.25 Ga. What kind of date is this?
cards.back: A model estimate conditional on the calibration: not an observed event and not a fossil floor.
cards.quote: That figure is a model estimate conditional on the calibration, not an observed event and not a fossil floor.
cards.section: The timeline in detail

cards.front: At Meishan, China, an age model places the end-Permian extinction between 251.941 ± 0.037 and 251.880 ± 0.031 Ma. Roughly how long did the extinction last in that section?
cards.back: 251.941 − 251.880 = 0.061 million years, about 61,000 years, in line with the 60 ± 48 thousand years estimated: brief on a geological scale.
cards.quote: Check their duration yourself: 251.941 − 251.880 = 0.061 million years, about 61,000 years, in line with the 60 ± 48 thousand years they estimated.
cards.section: Extinction numbers

cards.front: In the Pseudomonas fluorescens microcosm system, Kassen, Llewellyn and Rainey varied productivity and disturbance. Where was diversity highest?
cards.back: At intermediate levels of both productivity and disturbance.
cards.quote: Kassen, Llewellyn and Rainey (2004) then varied productivity and disturbance in the same system, and diversity peaked at intermediate levels of both.
cards.section: More on the flask

cards.front: Without fossils, how could a student still test the claim that speciation sped up recently in a clade whose tree of living species rises steeply toward the present?
cards.back: Justify a constraint from outside the tree: test a specific model, such as a speed-up timed to an independently dated event, and say the conclusion depends on that constraint.
cards.quote: Without fossils, test a specific model, such as a speed-up timed to an independently dated event, and say the conclusion depends on that constraint.
cards.section: A second design problem: a tree that rises toward the present
